Anvil Mobile Labs

Deconstruct the binary. Forge the payload.

How Anvil Mobile Labs works — the full flow, in plain language

Anvil Mobile Labs is a pipeline. You drop a package in at the top, it moves left-to-right through load → audit → decompile → deep-view → rebuild, and each stage feeds the next. Everything runs in your browser — no upload, no install.

1 · LOADAnvil section 1 reads the file and auto-detects its type. Binary AndroidManifest.xml (AXML) and Info.plist (bplist00) are decoded to text. Big archives (>2 GB) use a streaming parser.
2 · AUDITAnvil scans the decoded manifest/plist for risk (permissions, exported components, debuggable, cleartext, ATS policy, entitlements…). Results land in section 5, every step is echoed in section 2 log.
3 · DECOMPILEAnvil section 3 turns the package into a readable tree — apktool-style for Android (XML + smali), ipaforge-style for iOS (plist XML + Mach-O/class-dump) — zipped for download.
4 · DEEP VIEWAnvil section 4 lets you click into classes/methods (Smali bytecode) or Mach-O binaries (class-dump + hex + ObjC AST) without leaving the page.
5 · REBUILDAnvil section 6 re-encodes your edits back to binary, re-signs, and repackages — including streaming ZIP64 output for huge files.
6 · ADVANCEDAnvil sections 7–19 are the specialist tools: secret scanning, Frida hooks, WebUSB device bridges (Android ADB / iOS lockdown), deobfuscation, report export, APK v2/v3 signing, iOS provisioning, and Mach-O triage & readable dumps.

Tip: read the blue “what this does” note under each section heading below — they explain the role of that section in the flow.

Mobile Security Triage, Decompile & Repackage Tool — decompiles (apktool-style Android tree / Mach-O + class-dump for iOS), decodes binary AXML & bplist to readable XML, audits, edits, re-encodes and repackages .apk / .ipa — and exports the whole readable tree as a ZIP. 100% client-side.

🔒 LOCAL ONLY — nothing leaves your browser
Opens your browser print dialog — choose “Save as PDF” to keep an offline copy of the current audit, findings and log.
📐 Section Visibility — hide sections you don't use
Uncheck sections you don't use. Preference saved in browser. Default: hides 10, 12, 13, 16, 17 (niche tools).

1. Load package

Entry point of the pipeline. Accepts a full .apk/.ipa, a generic .zip, or a raw AndroidManifest.xml/Info.plist. The three buttons run the Android audit, iOS audit, or both. Feeds the log (§2) and the findings (§5) only — Section 3 stays empty until you Recompile.
Accepts a full .apk/.ipa (binary manifest/plist auto-decoded), a generic .zip containing either, a raw AndroidManifest.xml/Info.plist, or any raw blob handled by Anvil Core: bplist00 → editable Apple XML, minified JSON → 2-space beautified (with precise syntax-error location), classes*.dex → full dexdump + Smali-style disassembly. Format is auto-detected from the first 8 bytes, never the filename.
1A · Convert plist / JSON / DEX → human-readable text files — multiple at once, auto-detected from magic bytes
Batch text extractor. Pick or drop any number of files below — binary bplist00, XML plists, minified/obfuscated .json, Android classes*.dex, or any XML. Each is decoded in-browser and offered as a <name>.txt you can open in any editor; Download all packs them into one ZIP. Already-text files pass through re-encoded as UTF-8.

    Android output is an apktool-like decoded tree: AndroidManifest.xml and every binary
    res/**/*.xml re-rendered as indented readable XML, the resources.arsc string table dumped
    to res/values/resources-dump.txt, and each classes*.dex parsed into complete pools, classes, method signatures, and available bytecode in
    dex/*.txt and readable-dex/*.txt. With standalone full Smali output checked, every method body of every class is
    also emitted as Smali/disassembly under smali/. iOS output mirrors it:
    every binary plist converted to XML, the embedded.mobileprovision payload extracted, every Assets.car decoded to a catalog/rendition report with embedded images copied to images/, and each Mach-O
    binary (the app executable and every .dylib/framework) parsed into macho/<bin>.txt,
    class-dump.txt, plus a readable.txt that names the binary type (executable / dylib / bundle),
    recovers Objective-C interfaces with their methods, disassembles each method body to ARM64 assembly (for decrypted
    binaries), and lists Swift/C++ symbols. Android native libraries (lib/*.so) are parsed to
    libelf/*.txt with their exported/imported symbols; image entries are organized under images/ with an images/_map.txt lookup table for recompilation. Equivalent shell commands are echoed
    in the log so you can reproduce the run with apktool / ipaforge / class-dump / otool /
    swift-demangle.

    Combined structural + Objective-C hierarchy for each loaded Mach-O binary (header → load commands → segments → sections, plus classes → superclass → methods / ivars / protocols).
  

  

  

    Android: pure-JS Dalvik disassembler — parses the DEX string/type/proto/field/method pools and each method's code_item directly, then decodes bytecode into Smali-style instructions (covers the common instruction formats — 10x/11x/12x/21c/22c/23x/35c/3rc/51l, etc). This is a real disassembly of the bytecode, not a decompiled-to-Java reconstruction — control flow (if/for/while, exception ranges) is left as raw branches/labels, same as reading Smali from apktool.

    iOS: parses each Mach-O binary's header/load commands (architectures, segments/sections, linked dylibs) and recovers Objective-C class names + selectors from the __objc_classname/__objc_methname string sections — the same signal otool -l / class-dump surface. This is a class/selector-level dump, not decompiled method bodies (Swift/ObjC implementations aren't reconstructed — that needs Hopper/IDA on the actual binary).

      ⚠️ Jailbroken-only
    
  

  

    
    
  

  
  

    Large packages (64 MiB–50 GB): the file never enters RAM — only the ZIP directory is indexed.
    Recompile asks where to save and streams every entry straight from disk in 1 MiB chunks (Chrome/Edge), so nothing above ~80 MB is dropped. You need as much free disk as the package.
    Signed output uses the v2/v3-only scheme (the default tick): the signing block is computed in 1 MiB chunks and written in place, and the v4 .apk.idsig is emitted as a streamed Merkle tree. Ticking v1 (JAR) instead/additionally needs a full in-memory re-zip, so on this path it runs the bounded in-memory builder for small files and, for files over ~80 MB, stops with guidance instead of silently truncating. An APK whose rebuilt package data exceeds 4 GiB (or has more than 65,535 entries) uses a ZIP64 directory that cannot be v2/v3-signed in place — it is saved complete but unsigned with a clear warning (iOS has no such limit and needs no signing block). Huge Assets.car image re-packing is skipped on this path (the original asset is kept verbatim). Firefox cannot stream 50 GB; use Chromium.
    Re-encodes edited manifest/plist into real binary AXML / bplist00. Android signing now asks two separate questions: which schemes (v1 and/or v2/v3 checkboxes) and which key (auto debug key generated in-page — no certificate or keystore needed — or, optionally, your own .p12, parsed in-browser and never uploaded). A v1 JAR signature alone is enough for adb install / most third-party stores, but Android 11+ and Play refuse v1-only for apps targeting API 30+, so keep v2/v3 ticked: the engine emits a real APK Signing Block byte-identical to apksigner sign, entirely in-page. iOS fake-sign strips the existing _CodeSignature/
    and embedded.mobileprovision so a jailbroken device can re-sign with ldid; installable IPAs for stock
    iOS still require macOS + codesign with your Apple Developer cert (no browser can produce those).


    Every command from section 3's decode step is echoed again here as part of the round trip, plus the build/sign step —
    Android: apktool d → edit → apktool b → keytool/jarsigner.
    iOS: unzip → plutil → security cms (mobileprovision, read-only — not re-signed here) →
    edit → plutil -convert binary1 → zip → ldid. otool / class-dump
    are decode-only (inspecting the Mach-O binary) so they don't re-run on build, but are listed again below for reference.
  


  
  

6.1 vs 6.2 — which one do I use? Both generate a small descriptor file that points at an .ipa you host on your own HTTPS server; neither signs nor hosts the app. 6.1 builds an apps.json source feed so the app shows up in AltStore / SideStore (sideload via your Apple ID / dev cert). 6.2 builds a standard Apple manifest.plist for a direct over-the-air install link (itms-services://). Pick 6.1 to publish into a store app, 6.2 for a plain “tap-to-install” link. In both cases the IPA itself must already be correctly signed — that happens upstream in the iOS signing controls of section 6.

    6.3 · Mach-O Header Lab — flip MH_* flags / zero cryptid in-browser
    
Byte-level header surgery. Load a Mach-O slice (or borrow one parsed in Section 4), inspect its header, toggle flags such as MH_PIE (ASLR) or MH_ALLOW_STACK_EXECUTION, and set LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO(_64) cryptid — then download the patched binary. Only the exact header words are modified; fat/universal containers keep every slice offset intact. Note: the code signature covers the header, so a patched binary must be re-signed (codesign -f -s - / ldid) before it will execute on-device; the patch itself is perfect for static triage and tooling experiments.

7. In-browser grep & secret scanner


Find things fast. Run a custom regex — or one of the presets (AWS/Google/Stripe/Slack keys, JWTs, internal IPs, weak crypto, insecure storage) — across every file in the package.

  

    
    
    or reuse the package already loaded in section 1
  

  

    
    
    
    
  

  

    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  

  
Runs grep -rnI-style: recursive, line-numbered, case-insensitive by default, binary files skipped unless they're a recognized bplist/AXML (auto-decoded to text first). Media (images/audio/video/fonts) and nested archives are skipped by default — their payload is compressed, so grepping raw bytes finds nothing — and are itemized in the status line (hover it for the full list); tick also strings-scan skipped media/binaries to run printable-string extraction over them instead. Large archives are scanned in async chunks so the UI stays responsive. Packages loaded in section 1 are used directly — small ones decode once into memory (≤ 64 MB), larger ones stream entry-by-entry from disk — so IPA/APK of any size can be grepped with no re-upload.

9. WebUSB + ADB device bridge — Tier 2, no local software


Reach a real device, no adb install. Claims the phone's ADB interface over WebUSB and drives the protocol in-page: device info, a shell, push & launch of frida-server, and a tunnel to tcp:27042.

  

    Speaks the raw ADB protocol directly from this page over WebUSB. Requires Chromium (Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera) on desktop, a USB cable, and the phone in developer mode with USB debugging enabled. On the phone you'll see the standard "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on first connect — that's the real adbd, not a shim.
    Firefox and Safari don't ship WebUSB and will show a disabled Connect button.
    Android devices only — for iOS devices use §18 below.

10. Smali deobfuscation helpers — CFG + XOR string decrypter


Make obfuscated bytecode readable again. A CFG (control-flow-graph) builder plus an XOR string decrypter for reversing packed/obfuscated DEX.

  

    Paste a single Smali method (from section 3's smali-summary/*.txt or section 4's viewer) to build an ASCII control-flow graph of its basic blocks (labels, if-*, goto, packed-switch, return*).
    The XOR helper resolves obfuscated string arrays of the form const/16 vX, 0xNN / aput-byte and applies a repeating-byte XOR key.
    Android smali only — for iOS string recovery use §7's secret presets plus §16.
  

  

    
    
  

  

    
    
    
    
  

  






  
11. Exportable audit reports — JSON + HTML executive summary


Share the results. Download the full audit as JSON or as a printable HTML executive summary (engagement, severity breakdown, findings, secret-scan matches).

  

    Aggregates the current package name, findings from sections 1–5, the latest grep matches from section 7, and any APK signing-scheme detections into a client-deliverable report.
    JSON is stable-shaped for CI ingestion; HTML is a print-friendly executive summary with severity breakdown suitable to attach to a penetration-testing engagement.
  

  

    
  

  

    
    
    
  

  






  
12. Entropy & validated secret scanner — Shannon entropy + AWS/Stripe/GitHub/JWT checksum validation


Find high-entropy blobs (likely keys/tokens) via Shannon-entropy scoring, then validate candidates with checksums — AWS/Stripe/GitHub/JWT — to cut false positives.

  

    Sweeps every text-decodable entry of the currently loaded package (section 1 or the section 7 grep source). Flags high-entropy tokens (Shannon ≥ 4.5 bits/char over 20+ chars) and validates known secret formats:
    AWS access keys (AKIA/ASIA 20-char), AWS secret keys (40-char base64 with entropy gate), Stripe live/test keys (sk_live_/pk_live_/rk_live_), GitHub PATs (ghp_/gho_/ghu_/ghs_/ghr_ with base62 CRC32), Google API keys (AIza + 35 chars), Slack tokens (xox[bpoare]-), Twilio (SK+32 hex), JWTs, PEM private-key blocks, Firebase URLs, Azure connection strings.
    Contextual dedup and false-positive suppression are on by default.
    Binary entries (DEX, Mach-O, dylibs, .so) are covered via printable-strings extraction, and large indexed packages are streamed from disk.
  

  

    
    
    
    
    
  

  

  






  
13. Network Security Config & sink XREF — NSC parser + WebView/Cipher/Runtime.exec back-trace


Android network posture + sink tracing. Parses network_security_config.xml and back-traces dangerous sinks (WebView, Cipher, Runtime.exec) to their callers.

  

    Locates every res/xml/*network*security*.xml in the loaded APK, parses <base-config>, <domain-config>, <trust-anchors>, <pin-set>, and <debug-overrides>, cross-references the android:networkSecurityConfig attribute in the manifest, and highlights user-trust anchors, missing pins, and cleartext-permitted domains.
    The sink XREF pass scans the DEX summaries and any embedded smali for dangerous sinks — WebView.addJavascriptInterface, weak Cipher.getInstance modes (DES/RC4/ECB/NoPadding), weak digests (MD5/SHA-1), Runtime.exec, SSLSocketFactory with ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER, and reflection-based class loading — printing the caller class:method and a 3-line context window per hit.
    Android only — for the iOS equivalent (ATS audit) use §16C.
  

  

    
    
  

  






  
14. APK Signature Scheme v2/v3/v4 + zipalign — pure-JS/WebCrypto signing engine


Sign properly, at scale. Pure-JS/WebCrypto APK Signature Scheme v2/v3 signing (streaming, works >4 GB) plus zipalign — Play-Store-grade signing entirely in the browser.

  

    Reads a repackaged .apk (either the last recompiled artifact from section 5, or a file you upload), performs zipalign (4-byte alignment for stored entries, 4096-byte for lib/*/*.so), computes the v2/v3 signing digests over the aligned ZIP (SHA-256 Merkle-style 1 MiB chunking with the standard 0xA5 chunk / 0x5A top prefixes), builds the SignedData / Signer blocks, RSA-signs them with your .p12, and inserts a proper APK Signing Block right before the Central Directory (with the trailing APK Sig Block 42 magic and updated EOCD offset).
    The emitted block is byte-identical to what apksigner sign produces (this engine was validated against the real Android SDK apksigner) and passes apksigner verify -v --print-certs; a corresponding v1 JAR signature is also written when v1+v2+v3 is selected.
    APK only — .ipa input is refused; IPA signing needs Apple's codesign (see the §17 iOS workflow).
  

  

    
    
  

  

    
    
    
  

  

    
    
  

  

    
    
    
    
    
  

  

  
💡 Streaming sign computes the v2/v3 Merkle digest in 1 MiB chunks and writes the signed APK directly to a file you choose (File System Access API, Chrome/Edge/Opera) — memory-bounded, works for apps >4 GB. Generate apksigner command prints the exact apksigner/keytool CLI commands to run locally on a machine with Android SDK build-tools (needed if the target requires a real apksigner-verified signature you run outside the browser).

  
Detached APK Signature Scheme v4. Keep a v2 or v3 scheme selected, keep emit detached v4 checked, and the regular signing action emits <final-apk-name>.apk.idsig beside the final APK. The idsig contains the version-2 v4 hashing info, fs-verity-compatible SHA-256 Merkle tree/root, the matching v2/v3 APK digest, certificate, public key, and RSA signature. v4 is never emitted as a standalone replacement for v2/v3.









  
15. Mach-O binary triage — read-only structural & security-posture audit


Read-only security-posture audit of a Mach-O binary: PIE/ASLR, ARC, stack-canary, FairPlay encryption, code signature, and entitlements — a JSON dashboard, never mutates the binary.

  

    Drop an .ipa, unzips it in memory (JSZip), isolates Payload/<App>.app/<Executable>,
    and runs a read-only parse of the 64-bit Mach-O header + load command table — no bytes in the binary are ever modified.
    Reports DRM/encryption state (LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64), PIE hardening (MH_PIE flag), code-signature
    presence (LC_CODE_SIGNATURE, structural only — not cryptographically verified), and linked libraries (LC_LOAD_DYLIB).
  


  

    
    

      
Prerequisite: Decrypted Build Verification

      
    
        
  • App Store packages are natively encrypted by Apple's FairPlay DRM.
    • 
        
  • Sandboxed web environments cannot process encrypted Mach-O pages.
    • 
        
  • Deep code inspection requires a pre-decrypted payload (e.g., dumped via frida-ios-dump).
    • 
      

      

        This inspector still runs its own structural check for you: the DRM / Encryption card below reads the
        LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64 cryptid flag directly from whatever binary you drop, so an
        encrypted build will be flagged rather than silently mis-parsed.

    16. Mach-O → Human-Readable Converter & Readability Audit — otool/class-dump-style text + per-region readability check
    

    otool/class-dump-style text dump of every Mach-O slice, plus a per-region readability audit that reports what % of the binary is text vs. code vs. encrypted — so you know exactly what can and can't be read directly.
    
  
    
    Converts a Mach-O binary (FAT/universal or thin, 32- and 64-bit, both endians) into a
    fully human-readable dump: header + flags, every load command, segments/sections with
    protection flags, linked dylibs, symbol table, string literals, ObjC metadata, entitlements
    plist and encryption/code-signature state. Then runs a readability audit that reports,
    byte by region, what was convertible to text vs what is inherently binary-only
    (executable code, pointer tables, signatures, encrypted pages).

    16B. Dylib → Human-Readable Converter — LC_ID_DYLIB, dependencies, exports, symbols, ObjC, audit
    

    Dylib is Mach-O too — filetype MH_DYLIB (0x6) with LC_ID_DYLIB install name. This converter shows install name, current/compat versions, linked dylibs (LC_LOAD_DYLIB), UUID, encryption, code signature, segments/sections, exported symbols, Objective-C classes/methods, Swift symbols, and readability audit. Works for .dylib, .so, Frameworks/*.framework/* inside IPA, thin or FAT.

    16D. Dex → Human-Readable Converter — classes.dex → dexdump + Smali disassembly
    

    Dex triage — converts Android classes.dex, classes2.dex, etc. into human-readable text: dex header, string/type/proto/field/method pools, class list, method signatures, plus full Smali-style bytecode disassembly of every method body (real Dalvik opcodes, not Java decompile). Handles up to 5GB via streaming parser. Works for raw .dex files or dex inside APK.

    17. Deep Reverse-Engineering Workflow — Ghidra / jadx / Capstone / frida-ios-dump command generator
    

    Hand off to the professionals. Generates the exact commands to give the loaded package to jadx, Ghidra/IDA/Hopper, Capstone, and frida-ios-dump.
    
  
    
    This tool runs 100% in-browser, so it cannot host Ghidra's decompiler or Capstone's full engine.
    Instead it generates the exact commands to hand your currently-loaded package to the right
    professional tooling: jadx (Android DEX → Java), Ghidra / IDA / Hopper (native pseudo-C),
    Capstone (100%-coverage disassembly), and frida-ios-dump (decrypt FairPlay binaries so the
    tool's own ARM64 disassembler can then read the method bodies).
  
    
  
    
    
    
    
  
    
  

    


















    
  
    18. Browser-only iOS WebUSB + Frida — no relay, Node.js, or native helper
    
  
    
    Direct browser path: Chromium claims the iPhone's Apple usbmux USB interface, negotiates direct-usbmux v2, opens a virtual TCP stream to device port 27042, upgrades it to a WebSocket, and drives Frida from the embedded web client. All bytes stay between this page and the selected USB device.
  
    
  
    
    Requirements: desktop Chrome/Edge/Brave/Opera in a secure context, an unlocked iPhone connected by USB, and either
    frida-server on an authorized jailbroken test device or a Frida Gadget embedded in an app you are authorized to test.
    Close Finder, iTunes, Xcode, Apple Devices, and other usbmux clients before connecting because only one process can own the direct USB interface.
    Safari and Firefox do not expose WebUSB. A stock iPhone without Frida Gadget/frida-server has nothing listening on port 27042.
